Barre de fer, souvent aplatie et fendue par un bout, dont on se sert comme un levier. Pince des carriers, pince des paveurs etc.

examples.text: Un second soldat saisit la pince de fer des mains du mourant, et déjà il avait ébranlé la corniche, quand une flèche l’atteignit à la tête et le renversa mort dans le fossé.

Une pince peut être un simple pied-de-biche. La pince-monseigneur ou un monseigneur décrit par Balzac est un levier court à bout plat dont se servent les cambrioleurs pour les vols par effraction (Grand Larousse universelle).

glosses: Instrument de chauffage analogue à une grosse tenaille à large prise pour saisir, déplacer et remuer les bûches dans la cheminée.

examples.text: "Il faut prendre cette bûche avec la pince" (Académie française)

glosses: Petit instrument à deux branches qui peuvent être serrées ou rapprochées l'une contre l'autre pour saisir ou maintenir quelque chose en place, parfois avec ressort. Pince à cheveux, pince à épiler, pince à glaçon, pince à linge etc.

Outil ou dispositif. La pince est une sorte de double levier articulé autour d'un axe, sorte de tenaille comportant à la courte extrémité un bec ou tête permettant la saisie ou forte prise par rapprochement de deux mors, parfois avec deux mâchoires et deux manches ou branches, à la plus longue partie tenue en main ou par les mains. De taille et de forme extrêmement diverses, adaptées le plus souvent au métier ou au service mécanique, elles sont utilisées pour suppléer une manipulation manuelle dangereuse ou impossible et saisir, tenir, maintenir un objet, voire plier, arracher ou couper la matière de l'objet.

examples.text: pince plate, pince coupante, pince universelle, pince multiprise etc.
pince à dénuder, pince crocodile etc. pour les fils en électricité
Pinces de forgeron. Les taillandiers, les serruriers ont de grosses pinces pour tenir leur ouvrage quand ils le mettent au feu.
Les tapissiers se servent de fortes et lourdes pinces pour tendre les toiles et les étoffes qu’ils emploient.
Les horlogers ont de petites pinces pour prendre et mettre en place des pièces légères.
En anatomie et en chirurgie : pinces à pansements ou pinces à anneaux, pinces à dissection, , pince de Museux, pince de Hunter, pinces hémostatiques etc.

glosses: Action ou propriété de pincer, de saisir avec force, à l'image d'une pince.

examples.text: Cet instrument, cet outil n’a pas de pince : ne saisit pas bien.

glosses: à l'origine puis , Action de pincer quelqu'un, c'est-à-dire de le saisir, de l'arrêter.

examples.text: Craindre la pince, être menacé de la pince, Gare à la pince (Grand Dictionnaire universel de Pierre Larousse)

glosses: To take hold (of), particularly with the hand.

examples.text: That suitcase is heavy, so grip the handle firmly.
Unfortunately the glue didn't grip, and the whole thing came apart.
After a few slips, the tires gripped the pavement.
"Grip tightly on the rope!" — "I'm gripping! I'm gripping!"

When Timothy and Julia hurried up the staircase to the bedroom floor, where a considerable commotion was taking place, Tim took Barry Leach with him. He had him gripped firmly by the arm, since he felt it was not safe to let him loose, and he had no immediate idea what to do with him.

glosses: To figuratively take hold of or grasp.

examples.text: We need to grip this problem, not shut our eyes and hope it goes away.

glosses: Of an emotion or situation: to have a strong effect upon.

examples.text: As the water level began to rise, I was gripped by panic.
[…] I lost something of the stifling fear that had gripped me, and could listen with more ease to what was going forward.

glosses: To firmly hold the attention of.

examples.text: The movie gripped me from beginning to end.

glosses: A hold or way of holding, particularly with the hand.

examples.text: It's good to have a firm grip when shaking hands.
The ball will move differently depending on the grip used when throwing it.

glosses: Ability to resist slippage when pressed in contact with another object or surface.

examples.text: These tyres are worn out and don't have much grip.

glosses: A place to grip; a handle; the portion of a handle that the hand occupies.

examples.text: Near-synonym: handgrip

glosses: A device, or a portion of one, that grasps or holds fast to something.

examples.text: The unthreaded portion of the bolt's shank is called the grip.

examples.text: You're a real grip.

glosses: Control, power, or mastery over someone or something; a tenacious grasp; a holding fast.

examples.text: Dotcom mania was slow in coming to higher education, but now it has the venerable industry firmly in its grip. Since the launch early last year of Udacity and Coursera, two Silicon Valley start-ups offering free education through MOOCs, massive open online courses, the ivory towers of academia have been shaken to their foundations.

The current president toppled his uncle in a violent coup in 1979, before sentencing him to death by firing squad. Since then, he has consolidated his grip over the country's industries and is accused of diverting tax money into his personal accounts.
We need to get a grip on these spiralling costs.
in the grip of a blackmailer
to strengthen one's grip on a company

Instead England produced something that felt a little transgressive in this most controlled of stages, tightening their grip in a bruising first half, before freewheeling downhill in the second with their feet up on the handlebars.

glosses: Mental grasp.

examples.text: He's losing his grip – he's practically senile.
For God's sake man, stop panicking and get a grip of yourself!

A person responsible for handling equipment on the set.
As much as one can hold in a hand; a handful.

glosses: Archaic spelling of grippe (“influenza”).

examples.text: She has the grip.

It so happened that, during a stretch of inclement weather in the fall, Lester was seized with a mild form of grip. glosses: A small travelling-bag or gripsack.
